definition: Avoiding a direct answer or commitment, often to hide something.
example: When asked where the last cookies had gone, my little brother gave an evasive shrug and changed the subject.
nuance: A vague answer may simply be unclear, but an evasive one deliberately dodges the question; do not confuse it with invasive, meaning intrusive.
prompt: A reporter asks a town official why a budget report has gone missing.
options: The official's evasive reply praised the new park instead of mentioning the report.
The evasive reporter pushed into the official's private office without asking.
Her evasive answer listed every missing figure plainly, clearly, and in full.
The budget report seemed evasive because it was printed in a tiny font.
reasons: Steering away from the real question to dodge it is exactly what this word describes.
Barging in where you are not welcome is invasive, a look-alike word, not dodging.
A complete, straightforward answer is the opposite of sidestepping the question.
Small print makes a page hard to read; it does not mean anyone is dodging a question.

practice.prompt: A teacher asks a student why her science homework is three days late.
options: Rather than explain, Mia gave an evasive mumble about having a busy week.
Mia was so evasive that she confessed every detail before the teacher finished.
The teacher found Mia's evasive questions about his family rude and prying.
Mia finally handed in an evasive worksheet covered in neat handwriting.
reasons: A fuzzy excuse meant to avoid the real reason is a classic way of dodging.
Confessing everything at once is being frank, the reverse of avoiding the question.
Prying into private matters is invasive behavior, not avoiding an answer.
A worksheet cannot dodge anything, and neat handwriting has nothing to do with avoidance.
